thesis: Rosalind Franklin produced the clearest X-ray images of DNA, including Photo 51, which revealed its helix shape. X-ray crystallography, the method she helped pioneer, solved most of the protein structures that AlphaFold learned from to predict how proteins fold.

story.title: Photo 51
story.text: At King's College London, Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling shone X-rays through thin, stretched fibres of DNA. Photo 51 showed a sharp X made of smudged layer lines. Franklin measured such images with great care: the X meant a helix, and the spacings gave its 3.4 nm turn and the 0.34 nm step between bases.

story.title: A helix writes an X
story.text: X-rays scattered by a helix fall on layer lines spaced by one over its pitch, the length of one turn. The bright smudges step outward layer by layer, tracing an X whose arms sit at right angles to the strands. A longer pitch crowds the layers together. A missing fourth layer line comes from DNA's two offset strands.

story.title: From diffraction to AlphaFold
story.text: Decades of X-ray crystallography filled the Protein Data Bank with more than 200,000 solved structures. AlphaFold 2 trained on them and learned to predict how a chain of amino acids folds. Hassabis and Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Franklin worked on DNA and viruses, so the link is through her method.

hint: Drag the pitch and radius: the layer lines spread or crowd and the X opens or closes. Set the strand offset to 0 and the missing fourth line comes back.
